Validate · business data context

Business data map

The map describes the tenant control plane, access-validation data, operational logs, and asynchronous exports. It is based on the inspected PostgreSQL schema and application code; external workers and unverified state changes are called out explicitly.

How Validate moves data

Platform administrators provision tenants and their configuration. Tenant administrators manage branches, terminals, devices, application users, and products. Tenant API clients synchronize operational data and submit access checks. PostgreSQL holds the durable business and security records; MongoDB holds NR consultation logs; Redis is an optional cache; RabbitMQ and an external worker handle ATDP exports.

Business entities and relationships

PostgreSQL contains the durable business records below; __EFMigrationsHistory is migration metadata rather than a business entity. NR logs are stored separately in MongoDB. No table rows were queried while preparing this map.

Entity Business role Why it exists
Tenant Customer organization identified by its RNEC. Owns tenant configuration, operational resources, credentials, and exports.
Branch Tenant service location. Places terminals and their validation devices within a tenant.
Terminal Tenant workstation or endpoint assigned to a branch. Scopes device registration and access validation.
Device Registered device associated with a terminal. Provides device identity used by the validation flow.
User Platform-level account. Lets platform administrators manage tenants and global configuration.
TenantAdmin Administrator account scoped to one tenant. Manages tenant settings and operational data.
UserApp Application account scoped to one tenant. Supports tenant application access and synchronization.
Role Role catalog. Provides role vocabulary; its exact relation to each account type was not verified.
Product Tenant product catalog. Lets tenant users maintain the products available to their workflows.
Operator Global operator catalog and service configuration. Stores operator records referenced by tenant settings; direct runtime use is unverified.
Contingency Global contingency switch. Persists whether the platform is in contingency mode.
SystemSetting Global authentication setting. Supplies the platform failed-login threshold.
AuditLog Durable administrative action history. Records security-sensitive and configuration changes.
RefreshToken Refresh-session record for supported account types. Enables session renewal and logout revocation.
TenantApiToken Tenant API token record. Persists issuance metadata; the IsUsed lifecycle is not completed in the inspected code.
TenantApiPasswordHistory Tenant API password history. Supports credential history and reuse controls.
TenantSecretHistory Tenant secret history. Preserves prior secret history during credential changes.
AtdpDownload Tenant export request. Tracks an ATDP document request while an external worker processes it.

The main ownership chain is Tenant → Branch → Terminal → Device. Tenant also owns application users, tenant administrators, products, and ATDP requests. Terminal and Device carry tenant ownership in addition to their parent relationship. Refresh tokens can reference a platform user, tenant application user, or tenant administrator. Operator IDs live in tenant settings rather than a relational foreign key.

Tenant configuration

A tenant represents a client organization and is identified by its RNEC. Its Setting value is persisted as JSON rather than a separate relational table. The settings include validation parameters, credential/configuration data, and the main and contingency operator IDs. The API connection details are encrypted before persistence. Operator references are not protected by a database foreign key.

Tenant creation provisions an active tenant and its initial settings. Administrative changes are saved through the tenant service and audited. The schema enforces unique RNEC; tenant deletion is logical.

Branch, terminal, and device ownership

Branches, terminals, and devices belong to a tenant; a terminal is assigned to a branch, and a device is registered to a terminal. The database enforces tenant-scoped branch name/code uniqueness, tenant-scoped terminal name and MAC uniqueness, device-code uniqueness within a tenant, serial-number uniqueness across non-deleted devices, and at most one non-deleted device per terminal.

Branches, terminals, and devices can be activated or deactivated. Branch and terminal deletion is logical; device deletion is also represented by a soft-delete flag. The service prevents deleting a branch or terminal while active child resources remain.

Platform and tenant accounts

The system separates platform users (User), tenant administrators (TenantAdmin), and tenant application users (UserApp). This separates platform-wide administration from tenant-scoped access. Refresh-token relationships are optional and point to one of those account types. A role catalog exists, but the inspected schema and service paths did not establish how it is joined to each account type.

Failed-login counters and lockout behavior are applied by the authentication service. Tenant administrators are created with an activation token and a required password change; activation sets the password and clears the token. UserApp records support logical deletion.

Operator catalog and tenant assignment

Operators are managed as global catalog records, including a service URL. Tenant settings store main and contingency operator IDs. The IDs are JSON configuration, not relational references; the inspected backend did not establish a runtime call path that invokes an operator service.

NR consultation logs

NR consultation history is stored in MongoDB collections rather than PostgreSQL business tables: LogConsultasNR, LogPeticionesNR, and LogRespuestanoSatisfactoriaNR. The log service reads either the application database or a tenant-specific MongoDB connection, and repositories return paginated, filtered records for review and troubleshooting.

These records are operational evidence, not the source of truth for tenant, branch, terminal, or device ownership.

ATDP download requests

An AtdpDownload belongs to a tenant and records a requested export. The API creates it in Pendiente before publishing an asynchronous request. The external worker later supplies the document through an HTTP interface; this backend exposes the PDF retrieval path.

Provision and configure a tenant

  1. A platform administrator submits tenant identity and initial configuration.
  2. TenantController delegates to TenantService.
  3. The service creates the active tenant, persists JSON settings, and encrypts connection credentials.
  4. Credential and configuration changes update SQL history/audit records where applicable.
  5. The API returns the result to the administration portal.

RNEC uniqueness is enforced by the database. Operator IDs are stored in JSON settings, so the database does not validate that an assigned ID resolves to an operator row.

Create and activate a tenant administrator

  1. A platform or tenant administrator creates a tenant-admin account.
  2. The service stores an activation token and expiry, marks password change as required, and sends an activation email.
  3. The administrator follows a valid, unexpired token and sets a password.
  4. Activation clears the token and expiry and removes the required-password-change flag.

If email delivery fails during account creation, the account remains created and the response warns that activation mail was not delivered. The account can be sent a new activation message later.

Manage tenant resources

  1. A tenant administrator opens tenant-specific resource management in the portal.
  2. Controller/service pairs create, read, update, activate/deactivate, or logically delete branches, terminals, devices, application users, and products.
  3. Branch, terminal, device, and UserApp controllers also accept CSV imports.
  4. Database ownership and uniqueness constraints reject conflicting resource identities.
  5. Deletion rules protect branches and terminals that still have active children.

Authenticate a tenant client, synchronize, and validate access

  1. A tenant client authenticates with tenant API credentials; the service creates a token record and returns the protected response.
  2. Synchronization requests are decrypted, applied to supported tenant resources, and returned as encrypted responses.
  3. The validation service checks tenant identity, branch, terminal MAC, and device serial against SQL data.
  4. The endpoint reports whether the submitted tenant/device context is valid.

This repository's validation flow checks tenant and device access context. It does not establish the external biometric/identity-verification result; that processing path is outside the verified code boundary.

Review NR consultation history

  1. An authorized portal user requests log records with filters and pagination.
  2. The log service chooses the configured application or tenant-specific MongoDB connection.
  3. A collection repository filters and returns the requested NR log records.
  4. The portal displays the result for operational review.

These reads do not change the authoritative tenant or device records in PostgreSQL.

Request and retrieve an ATDP export

  1. An administrator requests an export for a tenant and date range.
  2. The API saves an AtdpDownload in Pendiente.
  3. The service publishes the request ID, tenant, and range to RabbitMQ.
  4. The external worker processes the request and provides the PDF through its HTTP service.
  5. The API calls the worker and returns the document or a mapped service error.

The SQL row is created before the queue publish; no compensating update was found for a publish failure. The queue consumer and subsequent status writer are outside this backend.

Change contingency configuration

  1. An administrator toggles the global contingency flag.
  2. The service persists the change and records an audit event.
  3. Tenant settings expose main and contingency operator IDs to the API client.

The flag's persisted transition is verified; the downstream decision to call a contingency operator is not established by this backend survey.

PostgreSQL

PostgreSQL is the durable store for tenant configuration, accounts, operational resources, authentication sessions, credential history, audit events, and ATDP requests. The inspected schema includes foreign keys and uniqueness constraints for tenant ownership and device registration. No live data rows were read.

The inspected backend references both PostgreSQL and SQL Server EF providers; the current schema inspection was against PostgreSQL. Provider selection across all deployments was not verified.

MongoDB

MongoDB stores the NR consultation, request, and unsatisfactory-response collections. Log queries can use the application Mongo database or a tenant-specific connection. MongoDB availability affects log review, not the PostgreSQL ownership model.

Redis and in-memory cache

Redis is optional. When it is unavailable, the application falls back to an in-memory cache. Cache invalidation failures are logged as warnings; Redis is not the durable source of tenant data.

RabbitMQ

ATDP requests are published after the request record is committed. A publish failure has no compensating state update in the inspected service, so the SQL request can remain pending without a delivered message. The queue consumer is not present in this backend.

External ATDP worker

The API calls the worker over HTTP to retrieve a requested PDF. Timeouts, connection failures, rejected responses, and invalid JSON are mapped to service-unavailable behavior; a missing NUT is treated as an empty result/not found. Worker deployment and export-status updates are outside the inspected repository.

SMTP email

SMTP delivers tenant-administrator activation messages. If initial delivery fails, the account remains in SQL and the API reports a warning; resend failures are logged and return a generic response.

Discovery gaps

  • I could not verify the RabbitMQ consumer or the process that changes ATDP requests after Pendiente.
  • I could not verify a runtime call path to an operator service, although operator records and main/contingency operator IDs are configured.
  • I could not verify the lifecycle of TenantApiToken.IsUsed; issuance writes false, and no update was found in the inspected backend code.
  • I could not verify how the Role catalog relates to each of the three account tables.
  • I could not verify the biometric/identity-verification decision path; the surveyed validation endpoint checks tenant, branch, terminal, and device context only.
  • I could not verify external MongoDB retention policy, deployed Serilog log destinations, or the sensitivity/retention rules for stored NR records.
  • I could not verify whether schedules, triggers, or queue consumers exist outside the inspected backend and live public database schema.
  • The OpenAPI MCP was unavailable for this run; the user authorized local controller and route inspection as the substitute. API contracts were not independently compared with a generated OpenAPI document.
  • The schema was inspected without reading business rows, so real-world data distributions and current record states remain unverified.
